title: Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
book_title: Chapter 3: How It Is Sold & Delivered — Distribution & Unit Economics
question: How does a tonne of PCBL carbon black travel from furnace to tyre maker, who sets its price and carries the risks on the way, and how much of each ₹100 of FY2026 sales survived as cash?

epigraph.quote: “And we are not chasing volumes. We would rather keep this capacity spare.”
epigraph.author: Raj Gupta, Chief Financial Officer, PCBL Chemical, Q2 FY27 earnings call, 2 November 2026

web_blocks.html: PCBL does not sell through shops, dealers or distributors. It sells a heavy, bulk industrial input to a short list of large manufacturers. Nearly every part of its economics follows from three facts. The buyers are few. The main raw material is an imported, crude-linked oil bought in dollars. The product travels by road, rail and ship at a cost that somebody has to carry. In FY2026 the company sold 618,956 tonnes of carbon black. Tyre grades were 354,841 t (57.3%), performance chemicals (non-tyre rubber blacks) were 194,480 t (31.4%), and specialty blacks were 69,635 t (11.3%) [15]. Domestic customers took 383,826 t and exports 235,130 t, or 38.0% of volume [15]. The Carbon Black segment earned ₹6,511.66 Cr, 79.5% of the group’s ₹8,189.30 Cr of FY2026 revenue. Aquapharm contributed ₹1,442.73 Cr and external power ₹234.91 Cr [3]. This chapter follows a tonne from order to cash and then follows a rupee of revenue to free cash flow. Chapter 2 describes the products and Chapter 4 the competitive position.

web_blocks.takeaway: PCBL’s protection is a pricing formula with a lag, not a volume commitment, and everything outside the formula is bargained order by order. That is how management can say that pass-through “works exactly as designed” on the formula book [39]. A quarter later, it says it is letting spot volume go [40].

web_blocks.html: On channel, the evidence points to a direct business. The October 2021 placement document recorded 89.69% of sales made direct and 10.31% through distributors and agents in the June 2021 quarter. It also recorded a sales force of only 41 people in March 2021 [47]. The FY2026 sustainability disclosure in the Integrated Report shows sales to dealers or distributors at 0.01% in FY2025 (four distributors) and not applicable for FY2026 [3]. The scopes differ, so we do not read a trend into the gap. We treat carbon black as direct business-to-business selling, with agents mainly in small overseas accounts and distributors mattering chiefly for Aquapharm [3]. Concentration is the real channel risk. Customers each above 10% of group revenue paid ₹1,958.55 Cr in FY2026, which is 23.9% of group revenue. The share was 28.9% in FY2025 (₹2,429.40 Cr) and 38.8% in FY2024 (₹2,488.75 Cr) [3][2]. Because each such customer is above 10%, there can be at most two of them in FY2026. The note gives only the total, and the name and count are not published. The wording looks loose, since the companion Chemicals line (₹147.66 Cr) is below 10% of group revenue. For FY2019–FY2021 the top five customers took 55.8%, 57.8% and 56.7% of revenue, and the top ten 64.8%, 66.1% and 64.3% [47]. That is an old but consistent picture of a short buyer list.

The contract language has also changed. The 2021 placement document said most customer arrangements were purchase orders. It added that customers typically did not enter long-term supply agreements and that PCBL could not benefit from a fixed price [47]. The FY2026 annual report says “a significant share of volumes flows through formula-based contracts with tyre majors” [3]. Both can be true, because a formula governs price and a purchase order governs quantity. What share of tonnes sits under written multi-year volume commitments is not published, and we would not assume it is high. Tyre-grade volume fell 17.0% in Q2 FY27 to 77,914 t from 93,892 t. It fell about 14.7% from 91,379 t in Q1 FY27. In that quarter, management says, tyre customers had stocked up ahead of a price increase and then destocked [18][40]. A buyer that can pull less is a buyer whose volume is not contracted.

web_blocks.takeaway: Capacity is quoted as “Equivalent Capacity”. That is the output a line could make if it produced only its highest-throughput grade, N330 on tread reactors and N660 on carcass lines. A changing grade mix therefore means real tonnes differ from nameplate [47]. Utilisation measured against nameplate is therefore a conservative number; Chapter 5 uses it with that caveat.

web_blocks.html: Feedstock sets the cost structure. Carbon black feedstock (CBFS), a refinery by-product priced off crude, is 90–95% of material cost. PCBL imports 90% of it and reports 75–80% from the US Gulf Coast [46][3]. Brent moved from about $60 a barrel in early January 2026 to above $100 by the end of March. Rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope added at least 14 days to shipping [3]. Management is now buying from several US vendors and is seeking Korean, Malaysian and Thai supply at a 1–2% premium [40]. One trading house supplied 8% of purchases of the main raw material [3]. The business hedges most net foreign-exchange exposure [46]. The net FX gain credited inside other expenses was ₹75.79 Cr in FY2026 (₹53.49 Cr in FY2025) [3], equal to 7.3% of EBITDA excluding other income. That is a recurring support but not an operating one.

Delivery costs are large and rising. Outward freight net of recovery was ₹206.70 Cr in FY2026, up 19.4% and 2.5% of revenue against 2.1% a year earlier; packing was ₹106.01 Cr [3]. If all freight were charged to carbon black it would be about ₹3,340 a tonne, an upper bound because Aquapharm ships too. In Q2 FY27 the MD said freight “risen very sharply with shortage of vessels” and that PCBL is “selective while logistics costs make the economics less attractive” [40]. On 29 July 2026 he added that PCBL gets surcharges from customers “in most cases” but not in full, “because we have to be competitive at a delivered price level” [39]. That is the commercial decision rule: quote, then decide whether the contribution after freight and feedstock is worth the tonnes.

web_blocks.title: Qualification: why the first order is slow

web_blocks.html: Tyre makers approve each grade at each plant before they buy. The Tamil Nadu plant shows how long that takes. On 17 October 2023 the CFO said: “The major hurdle now in way of capacity utilization, I would say, is approval from major tyre customers ... The normal process itself takes about two to three quarters time for all the approvals to come by” [26]. Until approvals arrived, output was “more of spot market sales and realization is a tad less” [26]. The plant ran at about 50% in its first quarter of operation, 60% in Q4 FY24 and 55% for FY2024 [26][28]. Approval is therefore a real barrier for a new entrant and a real delay for PCBL’s own new lines. The 90 ktpa added in January and March 2026 has not yet shown up in volumes, which fell 17% in Q2 FY27 [18]. The company has not said whether brownfield lines on approved grades clear faster.

web_blocks.title: Pricing, billing and the payment clock

web_blocks.html: The lag is easiest to see in Q1 FY27. Brent averaged $97 a barrel against $78 in Q4 FY26 [39]. Carbon black EBITDA per tonne jumped to ₹22,900 from an implied ₹14,000 or so in Q4 FY26 (our derivation from the full-year figure) [39][15]. The CFO said realisation per tonne rose about ₹27,000 quarter on quarter. Of that, ₹11,000–12,000 was margin from better spot pricing and the rest was cost pass-through [39]. Low-cost inventory added “close to INR70-odd crores”, of which management expected ₹40–50 Cr to reverse [39]. In Q2 FY27 only ₹10–15 Cr reversed because crude stayed high. The quarter also included a ₹33 Cr refund of US tariffs, or ₹2,300 a tonne [40]. So the swing of about ₹9,000 a tonne between Q4 FY26 and Q1 FY27 is mostly timing and spot. The more telling number is therefore the roughly ₹17,500 of Q2 FY27 net of the refund [40].

web_blocks.takeaway: FY2026 debtor days of 62 plus inventory days of 65, less payable days of 92, leave a 35-day cycle [4]. The sustainability disclosure gives payable days of 91 [3]. FY2024 and FY2025 are distorted because year-end balances included Aquapharm while FY2024 revenue included only about two months of it (₹239.07 Cr) [2][4]. Receivable terms are 0–90 days and payables 0–180 days. At March 2026, 83.9% of receivables were not yet due and no receivable was disputed or unbilled. The credit-loss allowance was only ₹3.51 Cr, 0.25% of gross [3]. Suppliers, not PCBL, fund most of the cycle. That works while crude is stable and flips when it is not (see Chapter 6 for the September 2026 balance sheet).

web_blocks.takeaway: The power business is tail gas that would otherwise be burned off, converted to steam and electricity at the plants. Its marginal cost is therefore small, and its output rises and falls with carbon black tonnes. The Q2 FY27 volume cut reduced generation to 186 MU from 223 MU [18]. The profit is real, but it is partly an arm’s-length sale to group companies and partly a grid-tariff windfall that management does not control. Read it as a supplement to carbon black spread, not as an independent engine.

web_blocks.takeaway: Company EBITDA per tonne multiplied by FY2026 volume is ₹924.7 Cr. That is close to consolidated EBITDA less Aquapharm’s ₹162 Cr (₹1,081.56 Cr less ₹162 Cr = ₹919.6 Cr) [15][3]. The segment-revenue column divides segment revenue by tonnes, so it is a rough realisation that includes small non-carbon-black items.

web_blocks.title: ₹100 of revenue to free cash flow, FY2026

web_blocks.html: The waterfall below uses one audited fiscal year, FY2026 consolidated, for the P&L and the cash flow. No trailing-twelve-month figure is therefore mixed with an annual one. Inputs reconcile to the audited statements. Revenue less cost of goods, employees and other expenses gives ₹1,042.97 Cr of EBITDA before other income, which is Screener’s operating profit. The company’s own EBITDA of ₹1,081.56 Cr adds ₹38.59 Cr of other income. Netting the ₹25.04 Cr Labour Codes exceptional charge against other income (₹13.55 Cr) is the treatment Screener also uses. It makes PBT tie to the audited ₹260.78 Cr and PAT to ₹198.04 Cr [3][4]. Capex is the audited gross cash-flow figure of ₹726.52 Cr [3].

web_blocks.caption: PCBL Chemical: ₹100 of FY2026 audited consolidated revenue (₹8,189.30 Cr) traced to free cash flow
web_blocks.takeaway: Of every ₹100 of sales, ₹69.83 went to feedstock and the inventory movement and ₹17.43 to staff and other costs, leaving ₹12.74 of EBITDA before other income. Depreciation (₹4.55) and interest (₹5.17) then took 76% of that EBITDA, so ₹3.18 reached pre-tax profit and ₹2.42 reached PAT. Operating cash flow of ₹19.25 is almost eight times PAT because interest is paid in financing, depreciation is non-cash and, above all, ₹6.46 (₹529.16 Cr) came from releasing working capital after crude fell. Without that release free cash flow would have been ₹3.91 instead of ₹10.37 per ₹100, and after interest and leases it would have been negative. FY2026 cash was strong because of a one-time release, not because the P&L earned more cash.

web_blocks.takeaway: The cash part of the order is low-risk and well run. The uncertain parts are the quantity the buyer chooses to pull and the lag between feedstock and formula price. Both showed up in FY2026 and Q2 FY27. That is why the per-tonne spread, not the tonnes sold, is the number that decides whether the business earns its capital.

web_blocks.title: What this means for an owner
paragraphs: PCBL’s distribution is a direct, low-cost and concentrated model. Customers above 10% of revenue are one or two names, the pricing formula protects the spread only with a lag, and about a third of volume is spot. The business is financed by supplier credit and was relieved of ₹529 Cr of working capital in FY2026 that will not repeat.

The unit economics are the next question: whether per-tonne spreads can hold in an industry with spare capacity. Chapter 4 tests whether the moat supports that, and Chapter 6 shows what the cash did once working capital turned.

book_paragraphs: Let us begin at the gate of a plant instead of in a spreadsheet. Picture a lorry arriving at PCBL’s Mundra works, which sits beside a port. Behind it, somewhere in a tyre factory, a production planner has noticed that his stock of carbon black is down to a few days. That is how this business works. Domestic tyre makers, the MD told analysts on 30 April 2026, keep only about three to seven days of cover. So PCBL is not selling into a warehouse; it is part of someone else’s production schedule, and the product, a fine black powder that makes up roughly a quarter of a tyre’s weight, has to arrive on time or a line stops. Now ask who that planner works for and how the price on the invoice got set. PCBL does not sell through dealers. A 2021 placement document recorded almost nine-tenths of sales as direct, a sales force of only 41 people, and a top five of customers that took more than half of revenue. The FY2026 accounts still show one or two customers, each above ten per cent of group revenue, paying ₹1,958.55 Cr, nearly a quarter of everything the group sells. You and I should hold that fact in mind for the rest of this chapter, because it explains why PCBL talks about contracts, formulas and pricing discipline in almost every call.

The contract is the part most investors misread, so let us be careful. The tyre makers do not pay a fixed price. They pay a formula that follows feedstock, with a lag. The MD put it plainly on 30 April 2026: “Some are Q minus 1, some are M minus 1.” That means the price this quarter is built from the cost of last quarter, or last month. When crude rises, PCBL’s costs jump before the formula catches up and the margin squeezes. When crude falls, the formula is slow to cut, and the company enjoys a gain on stock. Q1 FY27 was exactly that: Brent averaged $97, the spot third of the book captured “strong realizations”, and the CFO told investors on 29 July 2026, “This quarter we have some extraordinary benefit of low-cost inventory, which is unlikely to be repeated in subsequent quarters.”

Here is the subtlety, and I want you to hold on to it. A formula decides price, not quantity. In 2021 the company itself wrote that its customers typically did not sign long-term supply agreements and bought by purchase order. By 2026 the annual report speaks of formula-based contracts with tyre majors. Both statements can be true, and the company has not told us what share of tonnes is committed. In Q2 FY27 tyre-grade volume fell 17 per cent from a year earlier and almost 15 per cent from the previous quarter. Management says some customers had stocked up in Q1 and then destocked. That is what an uncommitted buyer does, and you should treat the pricing formula as protection for the spread, not for the volume.

The second half of the story is feedstock. Carbon black is made by cracking a heavy oil, called carbon black feedstock, in a furnace. That oil is ninety to ninety-five per cent of PCBL’s material cost, and about ninety per cent of it is imported, with the company reporting that 75 to 80 per cent comes from the US Gulf Coast. When the West Asia conflict began in February 2026, ships rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope, adding at least fourteen days, and Brent went from about $60 in early January to above $100 by the end of March. Freight costs rose too: outward freight was ₹206.70 Cr in FY2026, up almost a fifth. You can see why the MD, on 2 November 2026, called the shipping bill the reason PCBL is “selective while logistics costs make the economics less attractive.”

That sentence turns a supply-chain problem into a pricing decision. On the same call he admitted that, for exports, “in some cases, we don’t have freight on a pass-through basis.” So when a Sri Lankan or Vietnamese spot buyer asks for a quote, the company computes what is left after feedstock and freight. If it is thin, the order goes. The CFO described exactly this: the volume fall was “primarily a margin decision”, and “we are not chasing volumes. We would rather keep this capacity spare.” Notice what that costs and what it protects. It costs about a sixth of the year-earlier tonnes. It protects the spread, and it avoids selling at the margin into a market where, as the MD put it, “some people are chasing volume and I assume some degree of cash.”

Exports are where logistics turns into strategy, so let us spend a minute there. About 38 per cent of FY2026 tonnes went abroad. The United States is the instructive case. Through much of 2025 an American tariff of around fifty per cent on Indian goods made US buyers cautious; the India–US deal announced on 2 February 2026 cut it to 18 per cent, and PCBL later received a ₹33 Cr refund of tariffs it had paid. Yet on the November call the MD explained that large American customers still contract their volume a year ahead and worry that a tariff could snap back mid-year, so they do not want to give up local supply. PCBL’s answer is to promise them stock held in the United States, to build railcar facilities, since 40 to 50 per cent of US volume moves by rail, and to open a warehouse in Antwerp for Europe. You will notice that none of this is a product story. It is a story about being physically close to the buyer, and it costs working capital.

Next consider why a tyre maker does not simply switch suppliers, and also why PCBL cannot simply fill a new plant. Every grade has to be approved at each tyre plant. On 17 October 2023, when the Tamil Nadu plant had just started, the CFO said: “The normal process itself takes about two to three quarters time for all the approvals to come by.” Until then, the output went to the spot market at slightly lower prices, and the plant ran at about half capacity. Switching costs protect an incumbent. They also delay the return on any new capacity, which matters because PCBL added 90,000 tonnes in Tamil Nadu in January and March 2026 and has not yet reported the earnings from it.

Now let me give you the picture that the waterfall draws, because it is the clearest summary of the model. Take ₹100 of FY2026 revenue. ₹69.83 buys feedstock and absorbs the inventory movement. Staff and everything else, which includes freight, packing, stores, power and miscellaneous costs net of an FX gain, take another ₹17.43. That leaves ₹12.74 of EBITDA before other income. Then depreciation takes ₹4.55 and interest ₹5.17, so only ₹3.18 reaches pre-tax profit and ₹2.42 reaches the shareholders. If you stopped there you would think a thin-margin business had done a poor year.

Now look at the cash line, and notice how different it is. Operating cash flow was ₹19.25 per ₹100, eight times profit. Part of that is arithmetic, since depreciation is not a cash cost and interest is paid in the financing section. But ₹6.46 of it, ₹529.16 Cr, was working capital coming back: receivables down ₹427.55 Cr and inventories down ₹258.89 Cr as crude fell, offset by lower payables. The CFO explained on 3 February 2026 that it came “partly because of our being able to negotiate better credit terms with our vendors and our customers and better inventory management,” and “also because crude came down in this period.” A release caused by falling crude cannot repeat unless crude falls again. Without it, free cash flow after capex would have been ₹3.91 per ₹100, not ₹10.37, and after interest and leases it would have been negative.

Power is the one part of the model that works against the gloom. The furnaces produce a tail gas that PCBL burns to raise steam and electricity. In FY2026 the group generated 839 million units, used about 40 per cent on site and sold 511 million at ₹4.24 a unit, which is ₹216 Cr of revenue. The power segment made ₹238.59 Cr of pre-tax profit on ₹585 Cr of assets, a return of 40.8 per cent. Spread over every tonne of carbon black, that is about ₹3,855, roughly a quarter of the ₹14,939 per-tonne EBITDA the company reports. The caution is that more than half of the power revenue is sold to group utilities, and power volume falls when carbon black volume falls, as it did in Q2 FY27.

You should also know what the per-tonne figure measures, because it is the number management quotes most. EBITDA per tonne was ₹19,930 in FY2025 and ₹14,939 in FY2026, a fall of a quarter, while the segment’s revenue per tonne fell only about eight per cent, so the squeeze came out of the spread rather than the price. When I multiply the FY2026 figure by the year’s volume I get ₹924.7 Cr, and when I take group EBITDA and subtract Aquapharm’s ₹162 Cr I get ₹919.6 Cr. The two agree, which tells us that the per-tonne figure is not carbon black alone; it is everything outside Aquapharm, power included. Then look at the 2026 quarters. The ₹22,900 of Q1 FY27 carried about ₹4,500 a tonne of inventory gain, and the ₹19,800 of Q2 carried ₹2,300 of tariff refund. Strip those out and you are at roughly ₹17,500 and below. That is the run rate to hold in your mind.

Before we close, ask a simple question that the waterfall cannot answer: who is financing this cycle? In FY2026 the group collected from customers in 62 days, held stock for 65 and paid suppliers after 92, so trade creditors of ₹1,447 Cr funded about 60 per cent of the ₹2,419 Cr tied up in stock and receivables. That is cheap money, and it is why PCBL’s working-capital needs look small in calm years. It is also money that is lent against the price of crude. In my experience, you learn how comfortable a supplier-funded model really is when crude doubles, and I will show you the September 2026 balance sheet in Chapter 6, when inventories and payables both rose by close to a thousand crore.

Let me close by walking a single order through, as an average case. Approval takes two to three quarters. The price is set by a formula one quarter or one month behind feedstock. PCBL buys oil from the US Gulf on supplier credit, pays after about ninety-one days, cracks it into carbon black, burns the tail gas for power and ships from the nearest plant. The tyre maker calls off tonnes within days of use, is invoiced at the formula price and pays on terms of up to ninety days; on average, debtor days were 62 and the full cycle was 35 days. The cash part is good. The part that can hurt is how many tonnes the buyer pulls and how far feedstock moves before the formula catches up, which is why we keep asking about the spread per tonne and not the tonnes themselves.

What does this mean for you as an owner? First, the distribution model is efficient and low-cost, but it is concentrated, and the formula protects margin with a lag rather than guaranteeing volume. Second, supplier credit funds a large part of the business, which flatters cash flow when crude falls and consumes it when crude rises. Chapter 4 now tests how wide the moat really is, given an industry with spare capacity. And in Chapter 6 we will see what the cash did once the working-capital release ended.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: An old accountants’ maxim says that profit is an opinion and cash is a fact. PCBL’s FY2026 is a good illustration of why the maxim needs a footnote: the cash was a fact, but ₹529 Cr of it was a one-time fact. Judge this business on the spread it earns per tonne and on cash before working-capital changes, and treat a release of working capital as a favour from the crude-oil cycle, not as earnings power.

book_callouts.title: FORMULA PRICE, NOT FORMULA VOLUME
book_callouts.text: When a supplier says its contracts are formula-based, ask two separate questions. First, how fast does the formula move the price when costs move? Second, what obliges the buyer to take any tonnes at all? PCBL has answered the first (one quarter or one month behind) and has not published the answer to the second.
